blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Reflect on your own writing and judge it against the brief: its purpose, form and audience; explain how your choices fulfil it, with evidence quoted from your text.

blocks.heading: What a commentary is
blocks.text: A reflective commentary is an analysis of your own writing’s choices of form, structure and language, judged against the brief, and it is not a summary of what the piece says. It is analysis because it explains what the choices do: the commentary and the analysis of a stranger’s text are the same craft, with one difference — the text under the lens is yours, and you know what you intended, which is the thing to explain.

blocks.heading: Says versus does
blocks.text: The difference between what your text says and what your choices do is the whole space a commentary works in: the first is content, the second is craft, and the marks are for the second. "My piece tells the story of the festival" retells; "my piece opens in the middle of the dance so the reader arrives as a guest, which fulfils the brief’s focus on atmosphere" analyses — the choice, the quotation, the effect, the brief.

blocks.heading: Retelling and feature-listing
blocks.text: Two errors hollow a commentary. Retelling the content of your own piece tells the reader what they already know and analyses nothing — the marker has your text beside them, and the commentary’s job is to explain it, not repeat it. And a commentary with no quotation from the text it is about makes claims no reader can check: it quotes your own piece in short embedded stretches, exactly as an analysis of someone else’s text would. And a third error shadows them: listing the features you used — "I used adjectives and metaphors" — and stopping, which is feature-spotting in your own writing; the point is what each choice does for the audience and the brief. The fix for all three is the same: every sentence of the commentary names a choice, quotes the words, and says what they do.

blocks.heading: A commentary sentence, taken apart
blocks.text: Take the model sentence apart to see the moves separately. The choice: the direct address — a form-and-language decision about how the speech meets its hall. The quotation: ‘some of you have never known’, embedded in the commentary’s own grammar so the evidence arrives inside the claim. The effect: the closure is made to sound like a shared history being taken away, which positions the hall as defenders — the reader of the commentary is told what the audience of the speech was made to feel. The link: the brief’s demand for persuasion is served by that positioning. Four moves, one sentence, and the sentence is a template: any choice, any quotation, any effect, any brief, and the shape holds.

blocks.heading: The same craft as Paper 1
blocks.text: The commentary is the Paper 1 analysis turned inward: the feature-evidence-effect-link sequence is the same, the embedded quotation is the same, the analytical register is the same, and the errors that lose marks are the same — summary, spot-naming, stock effects, no evidence. What changes is the object (your own text) and the judge (the brief, standing where the source’s context stood). A learner who can analyse a stranger’s text can analyse their own; the only new skill is the honesty — explaining what you did, not what you wish you had done, which is why the commentary is written straight after the piece, while the decisions are still warm.

blocks.heading: Worked example: one commentary sentence
blocks.text: From a model speech: "The tricolon ‘we came, we saw, we were asked to leave’ undercuts the piece’s formality at the close, which fulfils the brief’s demand for a speech that entertains its hall while making its point." One sentence, all four moves: the choice (the tricolon), the quotation, the effect (undercutting formality, entertaining), the link to the brief. Twelve of these sentences, and the commentary is written — which is why the sentence shape is worth learning as a reflex.
